clue.text: Hyperion's widow married a satyr

parts.note: Hamlet compares his dead father to Hyperion and his uncle Claudius to a satyr; the queen, widowed, wed the uncle

explanation.surface: A sun god's widow takes a goatish woodland creature as her second husband.
explanation.walkthrough: Hamlet's line 'So excellent a king, that was to this Hyperion to a satyr' sets his dead father against Claudius; the widow is Hamlet's mother.
explanation.definitionFit: In Shakespeare's play the prince's mother is the queen who remarries her husband's brother within a month.

clue.text: Bauble the funny fellow West for instance put up

indicators.note: in a down clue put up means the whole sequence is written from bottom to top

parts.note: a wag is a joker
eg (exempli gratia) means for instance

explanation.surface: A trinket is set up by a comic, Mae West for example.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put up' reverses the run WAGWEG in this down entry. 'West for instance' suggests the comic actress Mae West.
explanation.definitionFit: A showy but worthless trinket or ornament.

clue.text: How the editor disturbed the peace

definitions.text: How the editor disturbed the peace

indicators.note: disturbed means thrown into disorder, so the letters of the word editor are mixed up

explanation.surface: A newspaper editor creates public disorder.
explanation.definitionFit: Running wild in a violent public disturbance is a way of breaking the peace.

clue.text: Musical girl loved calling Indian style

definitions.text: Musical girl loved calling Indian style

parts.words: Musical girl loved calling Indian style
parts.note: the heroine of the 1924 operetta is wooed with the duet Indian Love Call

explanation.surface: A girl in a show whose lover calls to her in the manner of the Native Americans.
explanation.walkthrough: The Friml and Stothart musical set in the Canadian Rockies is famous for its song 'Indian Love Call'.
explanation.definitionFit: The title heroine of the Rudolf Friml operetta sings the Indian Love Call duet.

clue.text: Maiwand casualty turned crime-writer

parts.note: Sherlock Holmes's companion was an army surgeon wounded at the battle of Maiwand in Afghanistan who then wrote up the cases

explanation.surface: A soldier wounded in Afghanistan takes up writing detective stories.
explanation.walkthrough: In A Study in Scarlet Holmes's friend was wounded at Maiwand (1880) before narrating the detective's cases.
explanation.definitionFit: Conan Doyle's narrator is the army doctor invalided home after Maiwand who chronicles Holmes's investigations.

clue.text: AA gun in ceremonial order

parts.note: ceremonial display is pomp
OM is the Order of Merit, a British honour

explanation.surface: An anti-aircraft gun drawn up for a parade.
explanation.definitionFit: The rapid-firing Vickers anti-aircraft cannon of the Second World War was nicknamed for the sound of its shots.

clue.text: Middle section of tome has its leaves out

indicators.note: taking the middle section means keeping only the central letters of the word tome

explanation.surface: The middle part of a big book has had its pages removed.
explanation.definitionFit: To omit is to leave something out or skip it.

clue.text: Knock-up fails to disconcert; opera hero

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the word for knock is written from bottom to top

parts.note: to rap is to knock

indicators.note: disconcert means unsettle, so the letters of the word fails are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: A tennis warm-up goes wrong but does not rattle the player, a heroic figure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' reverses RAP to PAR; 'to disconcert' scrambles FAILS to SIFAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Wagner's last music drama is named for its hero, the innocent fool who becomes Grail king.

clue.text: "Many a holy text That teach the rustic —— to die" (Gray)

definitions.text: "Many a holy text That teach the rustic —— to die" (Gray)

parts.words: "Many a holy text That teach the rustic —— to die" (Gray)
parts.note: the missing word comes from Gray's Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard, describing the verses on rustic gravestones

explanation.surface: A line from Gray's Elegy about texts on country graves teaching villagers how to die.
explanation.walkthrough: The full line reads 'And many a holy text around she strews, That teach the rustic ... to die'.
explanation.definitionFit: Gray's word for the countryman who draws lessons on right conduct from the gravestone texts is one who moralizes.

clue.text: From court many getting dismissed to a seat in the Lords

parts.note: to court someone is to woo them
L is the Roman numeral fifty, a large number
getting dismissed is getting the sack

explanation.surface: Many are thrown out of court and end up in the House of Lords.
explanation.walkthrough: The WOOLSACK is the wool-stuffed cushion in the House of Lords on which the Lord Speaker sits.
explanation.definitionFit: The Lord Speaker's red cushion stuffed with wool is the best-known seat in the upper chamber of Parliament.

clue.text: Paper that represents the left as right

definitions.meaning: the Daily ... is a British tabloid newspaper

definitions.text: that represents the left as right
definitions.meaning: a looking glass shows a reflected image with left and right swapped

explanation.definitionFit: A tabloid newspaper and a looking glass, which reverses an image side to side, share the name.

clue.text: Things that happen in dark rooms

definitions.text: Things that happen in dark rooms

parts.words: Things that happen in dark rooms
parts.note: events in general, and also what photographic film undergoes in a darkroom

explanation.surface: Something mysterious goes on in unlit rooms.
explanation.definitionFit: Events or happenings are this, and so is processing photographic film in a darkroom.

clue.text: A major optical fault on Jack's side

parts.note: in the Sermon on the Mount, the beam in your own eye is the large fault beside the mote in your brother's

explanation.surface: A serious flaw in a sailor's eyesight on one side.
explanation.walkthrough: Jack (Jack Tar) is a sailor, so his side is the side of a ship.
explanation.definitionFit: Nautically, something lying at right angles to a vessel's keel, level with the middle of her side, is in this position.

clue.text: Finished with the pipe-lighter, people needing resettlement

parts.note: something finished is over
a spill is a thin strip of wood or paper for lighting a pipe

explanation.surface: Done with the match, the smoker turns to a housing problem.
explanation.definitionFit: Population moved out of an overcrowded city into new towns was called surplus or excess population in postwar planning.

clue.text: Henry IV was one of these insomniacs

definitions.text: Henry IV was one of these insomniacs

parts.words: Henry IV was one of these insomniacs
parts.note: Shakespeare's Henry IV laments that 'uneasy lies the head that wears a crown', so kings are pictured as poor sleepers

explanation.surface: A medieval king is listed among history's poor sleepers.
explanation.definitionFit: Monarchs, each wearing a crown, are the subject of the king's complaint about sleepless royal nights.

clue.text: Sadness of poet listening to a nightingale

definitions.text: Sadness of poet listening to a nightingale

parts.words: Sadness of poet listening to a nightingale
parts.note: Keats's Ode to a Nightingale opens 'My ...', the poet's pain on hearing the bird

explanation.surface: A poet grows melancholy hearing a bird sing.
explanation.definitionFit: Keats's opening line names an aching of the heart, which is grief or sorrow.

clue.text: Egghead put on fantastic £300 tie, being choosy

indicators.note: in a down clue put on means placed on top of what follows

parts.note: the head, meaning first letter, of Egg

indicators.note: fantastic means wildly fanciful, so the letters of the money and tie are rearranged

parts.note: the pound sign gives L (libra) and 300 is CCC in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: An intellectual dons a wildly expensive necktie, being fussy about clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fantastic' rearranges LCCCTIE to CLECTIC, which goes under E.
explanation.definitionFit: Selecting the best from many sources, picking and choosing.

clue.text: Wax here before and after run

parts.note: in means at home, present here
in cricket a batsman stands at the crease before setting off and grounds the bat behind it after completing a run

explanation.surface: Polish is applied before and after a jog.
explanation.walkthrough: The CREASE is the line marked at each end of a cricket pitch; a run is scored by running from one to the other.
explanation.definitionFit: Wax is an old verb meaning to grow, as the moon waxes.

clue.text: Customary home for nuns by the island lake

indicators.note: by here means next to, putting the island straight after the nuns' home

parts.note: a convent is where a community of nuns lives
Iona is the Hebridean island of St Columba's monastery
L is a standard abbreviation for lake on maps

explanation.surface: A nunnery stands beside a lake on a Scottish isle.
explanation.walkthrough: IONA is a small island in the Inner Hebrides off western Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: Customary and conventional both describe what follows accepted habit or tradition.

clue.text: Put the old thing inside most 20 we hear

indicators.note: inside means one piece placed within the letters of put

parts.note: taken as written
res is Latin, the old classical tongue, for thing

explanation.surface: Put the old thing inside, most hunted, we are told.
explanation.walkthrough: 20 is CHASED; 'most chased, we hear' sounds like most chaste, the sense of the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Most chased said aloud is most chaste, which means most virtuous or unsullied.

clue.text: Huntsman's quarry thus portrayed on metal

definitions.meaning: the fox or deer is pursued by the hunt
a design engraved or embossed into silver or gold

explanation.definitionFit: Hunted game is pursued, and decorative metalwork tooled with a design shares the past participle.

clue.text: Sort of marrow the bird eats?

definitions.text: Sort of marrow the bird eats?

indicators.note: a sort of something is a variant of it, so the letters of the two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A garden bird pecking at a vegetable marrow.
explanation.walkthrough: Rearrange MARROW THE; the whole clue then describes the result, a long garden creature birds feed on.
explanation.definitionFit: Blackbirds and thrushes pull this soil-dwelling invertebrate from lawns, and its long body is a sort of marrow-like tube.

clue.text: Yankee Stadium's pigeon?

parts.note: a big baseball hit clearing the outfield fence and a racing bird that flies back to its loft share a short slang name

explanation.surface: A pigeon at a New York baseball ground.
explanation.walkthrough: Yankee Stadium is the New York Yankees' baseball ground, where a hit over the fence scores a run for the batter outright.
explanation.definitionFit: Baseball slang for a four-base hit is also the name for a racing bird trained to fly back to its loft.

clue.text: What the soothsayer said, as told in court

definitions.meaning: sooth is an old word for what is so, and a soothsayer literally speaks it
witnesses swear to tell the whole of what really happened

explanation.definitionFit: Sooth is archaic for fact, and court witnesses swear an oath to speak what is real and honest.

clue.text: Shock disrupts Sumatra — capital destroyed

indicators.note: to disrupt is to throw into disorder, so the remaining letters of the island are rearranged
the capital, meaning the initial letter, of the island's name is removed

explanation.surface: An upheaval on an Indonesian island wipes out its chief city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'capital destroyed' removes the first letter S of Sumatra, leaving UMATRA, which 'disrupts' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: A severe physical or emotional shock is the sense of the medical and psychological term.

clue.text: Adverse critics hammered at the doors

definitions.meaning: people who constantly run things down are said to knock them
door fittings that are struck to announce a visitor

explanation.definitionFit: Faultfinders who disparage, and metal rappers fixed to front doors, share the name.

clue.text: Pecksniff's stony-hearted Charity

parts.note: in Dickens's Martin Chuzzlewit Pecksniff's daughter Charity has a pet name, and a fruit with a stone at its heart bears it too

explanation.surface: A hypocrite's daughter is called hard-hearted.
explanation.walkthrough: Pecksniff's daughters Charity and Mercy are called by pet names in the novel; stony-hearted also points to a stone fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: Dickens gives Charity Pecksniff a fruity nickname, and that small red fruit has a stone at its centre.

clue.text: Gave Bill the last word

parts.note: a parliamentary bill becomes law only once the monarch's royal agreement is given as the final step

explanation.surface: Someone let Bill have the final say in an argument.
explanation.walkthrough: Bill looks like a man's name; it is a draft law, which needs royal approval last of all.
explanation.definitionFit: Agreed or consented, as the sovereign does to a bill in giving royal approval.
